catalog_quote: 2.4 Stress. Most unaffixed words consist of one or two syllables. The stress on a two syllable word generally falls on the first syllable. (56) /tɔwuŋ/ [ˈtɔ.wuŋ] 'egg' ... There is usually equal stress on both syllables when they each have the same vowel. (57) /ʌpmʌk/ [ˈʌp.ˈmʌk] 'cough' ... The weight of a syllable may also affect the stress on a word. The lightest of syllables are those with the short vowel, [ɨ]. If this occurs in the initial syllable the stress occurs on the next syllable as in (58). When the initial vowel is [ɪ], also very light, the first two syllables receive equal stress as in (59). (58) /bitsɛp/ [ᵐbɨ.ˈtsʲɛp] 'time' (59) /tsiwet/ [ˈtsɪ.ˈɥet] 'pit-pit' ... If the first syllable is a single vowel the first two syllables receive equal stress if the second syllable is CV or CVC as in (60). new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Nankina has an empty rule and no existing statements; this OPD supplies a placement (predictable, mostly initial). It is the SIL summary sheet whose data were checked by the same authors (the Spauldings) as the unobtainable 1988 Phonology Essentials, and its bibliography lists only the Spauldings' 1988-1990 manuscripts, so it is the closest available proxy for that work.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-contrastive) and usually falls on the first syllable of the word. The one-sentence statement gives no conditions for the cases where it does not fall on the first syllable, and says nothing about tone or length despite the section heading.
new_statements.exceptions: Implied only by 'most often': some words do not have initial stress, but no rule or examples are given.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD covers the Nankina language [nnk] of Teptep, Madang Province (Trans New Guinea, Finisterre-Huon, Yupna family; villages Bambu, Tempawon, Gumbaion, Gwarawon, MiokMambit); no dialect is distinguished. The 1988 report's SIL record lists subject language Nankina [nnk]. A Domung phonology thesis (twu_902) also sits in the directory from the compilation of 9/16; it is about Domung, a different Yupna language, and was not used here.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the scan we hold at the stated pages (book 17-19 = PDF 25-27; p.18 image read directly). (2) The source is the language's sole reference grammar (1994, vii+259 pp, first-hand SIL fieldwork) with a dedicated stress section; Glottolog's four descriptive refs reduce to this one work plus a phrase book, and a web search (SIL archives, TWU repository, Wikipedia/Glottolog trails) turned up no later or instrumental treatment. (3) The authors' own 1992 OPD sheet, downloaded now from the Internet Archive, independently states 'The stress is predictable and falls most often to the first syllable', consistent with the initial-default-plus-light-vowel-exceptions reading coded as weight-hedged (left edge, full-vs-reduced-vowel weight class); Moe's Domung thesis reads Spaulding the same way.
